newsitem.title: MEXICO: Amado Carrillo Fuentes: Mexico's top drug baron.
newsitem.headline: Amado Carrillo Fuentes: Mexico's top drug baron.

text.p: Mexican drug lord Amado Carrillo Fuentes, who died from a heart attack following plastic surgery, became one of the world's most powerful cocaine traffickers in the mid-1990s.

Nicknamed "The Lord of the Skies," Carrillo was known best for his use of passenger aircraft with stripped-out seats to transport up to five tonnes of cocaine at a time undetected from South America to Mexico.

This brazen tactic, and the demise of Colombian cartels in past years, helped shift the focus in the war on drugs from the jungles of South America to the deserts of northern Mexico -- on the doorstep of the United States, analysts say.
Thomas Constantine, the head of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), described Carrillo in June 1996 as "the most powerful figure in the Mexican drug trade".

Once just "mules" for Colombian cartels, Mexican drug gangs in the late 1980s began receiving payment in kind and set up their own distribution networks -- eventually eclipsing their South American counterparts in size and might.
A rising star among those was Carrillo's so-called Juarez Cartel in the northern border city of Ciudad Juarez, across from El Paso, Texas.

"(The shift) increased their profits by approximately 1,000 percent (and) launched these already formidable crime syndicates on the road to enormous fortunes," Constantine testified to U.S. legislators.

U.S. officials estimated the Juarez cartel's revenues from drug-trafficking at several million dollars a week -- nearly a third of which was used to bribe government officials on both sides of the border, experts say.

Believed to be a nephew of jailed Guadalajara cartel drug kingpin Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, Carrillo seized control of the Juarez gang in April 1993, when its previous head, Rafael Aguilar Guajardo, was murdered in the Mexican tourist resort of Cancun.

Carrillo, 42, finally rose to the top of the trafficking heap following the 1996 capture of rival Gulf Cartel kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego, arrested in 1996 and now serving a life sentence without parole in a U.S. prison.
"He moves four times more than other Mexican traffickers," a U.S. official said of Carrillo in 1995. "He handles $60 million in cash the way you or I handle $5."

Sure of protection at a price, Carrillo became more daring, building a fantasy palace in Hermosillo, Sonora state, just a few blocks down from the homes of the state governor and the U.S. consul. The property was eventually seized.
Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, Mexico's top anti-drug official and a man widely praised by U.S. officials, was arrested in February on charges he was on Carrillo's payroll.

Carrillo's gang preferred to use dollar bills instead of bullets to get its way, but it did have a brutal streak. On one occasion U.S. drugs agents in El Paso found three bodies in a car trunk with yellow muzzles tied to their mouths, in what they took to be a "gift" from the capo.

When Carrillo's pet tiger escaped earlier this year in Ciudad Juarez -- and police angered the capo by handing the tiger over to a zoo -- the cartel's victims began turning up tied in yellow ribbons emblazoned with the image of a tiger.

Carrillo earned a reputation for narrow escapes. Rival mobsters surprised him as he calmly ate at a Mexico City restaurant in 1993, but Carrillo escaped through a toilet window amid a hail of bullets.
Earlier this year, Carrillo escaped an army raid on his sister's wedding in the northern Sinaloa state thanks to a tip from an army major, who was later arrested.
Carrillo was arrested once -- on August 21, 1989 -- in Guadalajara but was released within weeks, further fanning suspicions that he enjoyed protection in high places.
Also known as the "capo without a face" -- he has rarely been photographed -- Carrillo was indicted in Dallas and Miami and had been a fugitive since 1988.
Following the Gutierrez scandal, U.S. pressure on Mexico mounted to capture the kingpin.

It is unclear whether he was having plastic surgery to help him evade Mexican authorities who may have been closing in on him, or to help him leave the business that gave him wealth, fame, and eventually death.
